title: Methods: Teach an Object What It Can Do
excerpt: Add methods to a class so objects can act on their own data, change their state and return results, and see what self really does.

headings.text: What Python Does Behind the Scenes
Methods That Change Data and Methods That Return It
Protecting the Object From Bad Requests
Each Object Keeps Its Own Data

html:
An object that only stores data is little more than a dictionary with a nicer name. The real benefit of a class appears when the object also knows how to do things with its own data: a bank account that can take a deposit, a dog that can speak, a shopping cart that can add up its own total.

A method is a function defined inside a class that works on the object it is called on. This lesson builds a small bank account class step by step, so you can see methods change data, return results, call each other and protect the object from invalid actions.

A Class With Methods

__init__ is a special method that runs when an object is created and stores its starting data, and balance=0 is a default value used when none is given. Each method takes self as its first parameter, which gives it access to the object's own attributes (+= means "add to the existing value"):

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount

    def summary(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance}"

acct = Account("Asha", 100)
acct.deposit(50)

print(acct.balance)
print(acct.summary())
150
Asha: 150

Look at the call acct.deposit(50): it passes one argument, but the definition has two parameters, self and amount. Why the difference? When you call a method through an object, Python fills in self with that object for you. You only supply the rest.

What Python Does Behind the Scenes

The call acct.deposit(25) is shorthand for calling the function stored in the class and handing it the object explicitly. Both lines do exactly the same thing:

Account.deposit(acct, 25)
print(acct.balance)

acct.deposit(25)
print(acct.balance)
175
200

Seeing it written out makes it clear that self is not magic: it is simply the object in front of the dot. (Each call added 25, which is why the balance grew from one print to the next.)

Methods That Change Data and Methods That Return It

The two methods above behave differently. deposit changes the object and returns nothing, while summary changes nothing and returns text. Check what a method without a return gives back:

result = acct.deposit(10)

print(result)
print(acct.balance)
None
210

The result is None, but the balance really did change. A useful habit is to make each method do one of the two jobs: change the object, or report on it.

Methods Can Call Other Methods

Inside a method, self lets you reach the object's other methods too. Here is a longer version of the class, with a method that builds on deposit:

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount

    def apply_interest(self, rate):
        self.deposit(self.balance * rate)

savings = Account("Ravi", 200)
savings.apply_interest(0.25)

print(savings.balance)
250.0

The method apply_interest works out the interest from the current balance and hands it to deposit, so the rule for adding money lives in just one place. (Multiplying by 0.25 makes the result a decimal, which is why the balance now shows 250.0.)

Protecting the Object From Bad Requests

Someone may try to withdraw more than the balance. A method can refuse with raise, which stops the method with an error (ValueError means the value is unacceptable), and leave the object untouched:

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds")
        self.balance -= amount

wallet = Account("Meena", 80)
wallet.withdraw(500)
ValueError: Insufficient funds

Why raise an error instead of just printing a message? Because the code that called withdraw can then decide what to do about the problem. The balance is also safe: the check happens before any change is made.

print(wallet.balance)
wallet.withdraw(30)
print(wallet.balance)
80
50

Each Object Keeps Its Own Data

Methods always act on the object they were called on, so two objects never interfere with each other:

first = Account("Asha", 100)
second = Account("Ravi", 100)

first.deposit(40)

print(first.balance, second.balance)
140 100

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonMethods.ipynb.

Summary

  • A method is a function defined inside a class; its first parameter is self.
  • In obj.method(x), Python passes obj as self automatically; it is shorthand for Class.method(obj, x).
  • Methods can change the object's attributes or return information about them; a method with no return gives None.
  • Inside a method, self.other_method() calls another method of the same object.
  • A method can raise an error to reject invalid requests before changing anything.
  • Every object keeps its own data, so calling a method on one object does not affect another.
